name: Shoe trees + polish kit
lead: Shoe trees and a polish kit keep leather shoes looking sharp. Polish restores colour, covers scuffs and adds shine, while shoe trees hold the shoe's shape and smooth out the creases that wear puts in the leather, so a pair looks cared for and lasts longer [1][3].

A shoe tree is a foot-shaped device placed inside a shoe to preserve its shape, limit creasing and extend its life. Wikipedia adds that trees also draw out moisture from sweat, which it describes as a major cause of lining rot and leather degradation, and that better trees are made of cedar or another softwood that helps control odour [1]. A polish kit typically pairs brushes, cream and wax. Wikipedia describes shoe polish as a waxy paste, cream or liquid used to shine, waterproof and restore leather shoes, which extends their life [3].

In style communities, well-kept shoes are described as a detail other people notice and read as a sign of care. No study located measures how observers judge polished versus unpolished footwear. One small laboratory study examined whether shared cedar shoe trees can transmit microbes between wearers [2].
infobox: Cedar or other softwood; plastic or sheet metal [1]

paras: Wikipedia groups wooden shoe trees into three broad classes tied to price and quality. Spring trees are the cheapest, lack a full heel, and are popular for high heels because of their flexibility, though the narrow heel knob can put excess pressure on one section of the heel. Generic trees are non-lasted and designed to fit many styles; twin-tube versions are popular in England and Europe and single-tube split-toe versions in the United States. Lasted trees, matching the last of a specific shoe, are at the top of the range.[1]

Plastic or stamped-metal trees are cheaper and lighter and are often used for travel, though Wikipedia says they do not absorb moisture the way wood does and that wooden trees can damage leather in luggage. Boot trees are a taller variant that support the heel counter and the shaft of ankle boots.[1]

A tree holds the leather in its intended shape while the shoe dries, which is said to stretch out creases formed during wear. Because wood draws moisture from leather faster than evaporation alone, Wikipedia says a tree aims to limit bacterial growth in sweat-saturated leather, and recommends inserting one soon after the shoe is taken off.[1]

Polish serves a separate role. In shoe-care practice, creams are said to condition and colour leather, and waxes to fill scuffs and give a shine. This description reflects general shoe-care practice; no studies on shoe polish and leather condition were located.

Wikipedia describes three families of shoe polish. Wax polishes are mostly solvent (about 70%) with 20 to 40% waxes such as carnauba and montan plus dyes, and harden after application to hold their gloss. Cream-emulsion polishes use water or oil with a solvent, held together by emulsifiers. Liquid polishes come in squeezable bottles with sponge applicators, have low wax content, and are cited by experts as able to dry out and crack leather with long-term use [3].

Polish is applied to clean, dry shoes with a cloth, brush or fingers and buffed with a clean cloth. 'Spit' or 'bull' polishing adds a drop of water for a mirror finish valued in military settings, and carnauba-based polishes can also act as a protective coating. Wikipedia notes polish is not a cleaning product [3].

Natural waxes, fats and oils were used on leather in ancient and medieval times, and demand for glossy finishes grew in the 18th century. Thomas and Jonathan Warren began making blacking in London around 1795 to 1798, and Charles Dickens worked at the Warren factory as a child [3][4]. Kiwi boot polish was started in Melbourne in 1904 by William Ramsay and Hamilton McKellan and spread through Allied militaries in the world wars [3].

Street shoeshining flourished from the late 19th century, and since 2017 the World Championships in Shoe Shining have been held in London, where contestants have 20 minutes to shine one shoe to a jury [4].

Evidence for the shape-preserving and moisture-absorbing effects consists of manufacturer and craft descriptions rather than published trials. The visual effect of polishing is immediate but temporary. No study located measures how observers judge a person who wears polished or well-kept shoes.

A 1998 study in the Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association tested whether microorganisms could pass between people through shared cedar shoe trees. It found that bacteria and bacterial spores were transmitted, fungi were not, and that only several hundred to several thousand pathogenic bacteria moved between any two shoes.[2]

Craft guidance also notes that the wrong polish or poor technique can stain or dry leather, and that some shoes need specific care. Wikipedia advises that plastic trees are better suited to travel than wood.[1]

Wikipedia notes that polish fumes can irritate skin, eyes and throat and that prolonged occupational exposure in shoe production has been linked to a higher risk of nose and sinus cancer, while general risks from normal use are considered low [3].

In style communities, well-kept shoes are described as something other people notice and read as a sign of care; the wiki's own summary line says people read shoes. This is a characterisation of community views; no study was found that tests it. Shoe-care routines are discussed alongside general grooming and dress.

No studies found on shoe trees or polish and appearance. The one related laboratory study found in the literature examined microbial transmission through shared cedar shoe trees and is described under Safety and risks.[2]

chain: Polish cleans, recolours and adds shine to leather
Trees hold shape and smooth creases while shoes rest
Shoes look neat, maintained and last longer
angle.text: Polish gives scuffed leather an even colour and gloss, and trees keep the toe box and vamp from collapsing into deep creases. Together they make an outfit's shoes look sharp and extend the pair's wearable life.
